TITLE: Quantifying Informativeness in Prompt-Based Rollouts
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of temporally-weighted“rule-of-thumb” heuristics to estimate a prompt's informativeness. Specifically, propose a composite metric that combines the model's past accuracy, the variance of the rollout groups, and the absolute advantage of the rollouts to estimate the signal strength contributed to the policy update.
CONTROLS: Baseline on uniform rollout allocation, ablation study to quantify the effect of individual heuristics.
COST: Preliminary estimates suggest 200 GPU-hours (4 pilot runs × 50 hours each) to gather satisfactory results.
PREDICTION: This will result in improved rollout allocation, allowing the model to capture hardest-to-reason tasks and shift computational budget to less informative prompts. TITLE: Revising Mutual Information as a Prompt Informativeness Metric
PROPOSAL: REVISED version of 1, we develop a revised metric based on the mutual information between the policy’s rollout distribution and its parameters. TITLE: Adaptive Rollout Sampling via Dynamic Difficulty Estimation
PROPOSAL: Develop a dynamic difficulty estimation mechanism that predicts the informativeness of rollouts for each prompt based on past rollout successes and failures. This is achieved by learning a parametric difficulty distribution using a probabilistic risk model (PRM). The difficulty distribution is then used to dynamically adjust the rollout sampling budget for each prompt, prioritizing those with high predicted difficulty.
CONTROLS: Baseline on uniform rollout allocation and constant difficulty distribution.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours for implementing the PRM and dynamic difficulty estimation.
PREDICTION: Outperforms uniform rollout allocation by allocating more resources to high-difficulty prompts: could fail due to overfitting of the difficulty distribution.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Rollout Sampling via Dynamic Difficulty Estimation
PROPOSAL: REVISED version of 2, incorporate a meta-learning component into the difficulty estimation process. By learning a meta-policy that adapts to the model's performance across different prompts and rollouts, the dynamic difficulty estimation mechanism can learn to automatically adjust its parameters to better suit the changing behavior of the model. This is achieved by using an episodic memory to store past experiences and update the meta-policy using meta-gradient descent.
CONTROLS: Ablation study to isolate the improvements contributed by the meta-learning component and compare to non-meta-learning version.
COST: Estimated 500 additional GPU-hours for implementing the meta-learning framework.
PREDICTION: Improved rollout allocation by adaptively adjusting to the model's evolving behavior, reducing the need for frequent updates to the difficulty distribution: could fail due to overemphasis on recent experiences vs long-term performance trends.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-based Prompt Informativeness Analysis
PROPOSAL: Establish a connection between the informativeness of a prompt and the gradient of the policy's loss function with respect to its parameters. This is achieved by analyzing how the gradient of the loss function changes as a function of the policy's rollout distribution and the prompt's rollouts. By identifying patterns in the gradient that are indicative of high-informativeness prompts, we can develop a principled method for allocating rollouts to prompts based on their informativeness.
CONTROLS: Baseline on uniform rollout allocation and ablation study to compare to KL-DIV-AIW-based informativeness metric.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours for implementing the gradient-based analysis.
PREDICTION: Gradient-based analysis can effectively identify high-informativeness prompts and allocate rollouts accordingly, potentially outperforming both uniform rollout allocation and KL-DIV-AIW: might fail to generalize across different model architectures and tasks due to sensitivity to loss function and gradient magnitudes.

TITLE: Adaptive Rollout Sampling via Dynamic Difficulty Estimation
PROPOSAL: REVISED version of 2, incorporate insights from gradient-based prompt informativeness analysis into the dynamic difficulty estimation mechanism. By using the gradient of the loss function as a feature in the difficulty distribution model, we can capture more nuanced relationships between prompts and their informativeness. This is achieved by incorporating a gradient-based transformation into the feature space used by the PRM.
CONTROLS: Ablation study to isolate the improvements contributed by incorporating gradient-based features and compare to non-gradient-based version.
COST: Additional estimated 100 GPU-hours for implementing the gradient-based feature transformation.
PREDICTION: Enhanced dynamic difficulty estimation by capturing complex relationships between prompts and informativeness, leading to improved rollout allocation: could fail if overly sensitive to noise in gradient estimates or if gradient-based features dominate other informative features.

TITLE: Model-Agnostic Rollout Allocation via Optimal Transport
PROPOSAL: Use optimal transport theory to develop a model-agnostic rollout allocation framework that can adapt to different model architectures and tasks. By mapping the embedding spaces of prompts and rollouts to a common transport distance metric, we can efficiently compute the optimal rollout allocation that maximizes informativeness while respecting the rollout budget.
CONTROLS: Baseline on uniform rollout allocation and ablation study to compare to KL-DIV-AIW-based informativeness metric.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours for implementing the optimal transport framework and computing transport distances.
PREDICTION: Model-agnostic rollout allocation framework can achieve improved performance across different models and tasks, leveraging the power of optimal transport to allocate rollouts effectively: might fail to scale with the size of the embedding spaces or when dealing with high-dimensional data.

TITLE: Offline Evaluating and Improving Rollout Allocation Methods
PROPOSAL: Design a comprehensive evaluation framework to compare the rollout allocation methods proposed in this work and existing state-of-the-art methods on mathematical reasoning and retrieval-augmented multi-hop question answering tasks. This framework includes offline metrics for evaluating rollout allocation policies, such as optimality, sample efficiency, and model performance. By analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of each policy, we can identify opportunities for improvement and further research directions.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing state-of-the-art rollout allocation methods and baseline rollout allocation policies.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours for implementation and evaluation of the proposed framework and comparison with baselines.
PREDICTION: Comprehensive evaluation framework will provide valuable insights for selecting and improving rollout allocation methods, driving progress in efficient and informative rollout allocation for complex tasks: might fail if the selected offline metrics do not accurately reflect online performance or rollout allocation requirements.

TITLE: Adaptive Rollout Budget Allocation using Reward-Informed Difficulty Prediction
PROPOSAL: This proposal involves developing an estimator for prompt difficulty using past rewards and a learned predictor, which can be computed quickly and reliably. Based on this difficulty estimate, we will develop a dynamic rollout budget allocation scheme that adjusts the number of rollouts sampled for each prompt according to its estimated informativeness. For example, difficult prompts that require more accurate rollout generation would be allocated a larger share of the rollout budget, while easy prompts would be allocated fewer resources. We will integrate this adaptive allocation scheme with a critic-free reinforcement learning algorithm such as RLOO.
CONTROLS: Baseline: uniform rollout budget allocation; Ablation: no difficulty estimation and fixed allocation, RLOO with uniform allocation (to account for sequential sampling efficiency gains).
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (~1 week of single-GPU training time).
PREDICTION: This adaptive rollout budget allocation should reduce the total number of required rollouts, improve training efficiency, and lead to faster convergence. However, it may fail if the learned predictor has high variance or difficulty estimates are noisy.

TITLE: Estimating Informativeness using Past Rewards and Gradient Quality
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether the quality of past rewards and the magnitude of gradients during training can serve as indicators of prompt informativeness. Specifically, we will analyze how past rewards and gradient norms for each prompt are related to subsequent rollout quality and policy update progress. This will help identify a principled metric that captures how much a prompt's rollouts actually help the policy update.
CONTROLS: Abstraction: analysis of existing datasets and metrics; Control: train and test split of prompts and data.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (~1 GPU-day of computation time for analysis and visualization).
PREDICTION: We expect to find some correlation between past rewards, gradient norms, and rollout quality, but may find difficulty in establishing a robust and scalable metric.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Threshold-based Rollout Pruning and Prompt Selection
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of inefficient rollout generation and slow training progress, we will explore a threshold-based approach to pruning rollouts and selecting prompts. The idea is to set a threshold for rollout quality, e.g., a minimum desired reward or a required variance in the rollout returns. We will then use this threshold to discard rollouts below it and focus on generating more rollouts for high-quality prompts. This will be evaluated against.heuristic-based methods (e.g., retaining highest-variance rollouts) and uniform rollout allocation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: uniform rollout allocation; Ablation: no pruning or selection; Comparison: heuristic-based rollout selection.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (~5 GPU-days of computation time for exploring different rollout budgets and thresholds).
PREDICTION: This pruning and selection approach should reduce the number of required rollouts and training time, but may fail to allocate sufficient rollouts to informative prompts, leading to suboptimal policy updates.

TITLE: Model-Agnostic Prompt Difficulty Estimation using Learnable Predictors
PROPOSAL: To decouple the difficulty estimation process from the specific model or task, we will develop a learnable predictor that can estimate prompt difficulty in a model-agnostic manner. This predictor will be trained on a variety of model outputs and tasks, and will learn to generalize across different models and domains. We will evaluate this approach on a range of tasks and models to demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness.
CONTROLS: Baseline: model-specific difficulty estimation; Comparison: learned predictor trained on a specific model or task.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (~20 GPU-days of computation time for training and evaluating the learnable predictor).
PREDICTION: This model-agnostic predictor should provide a robust and generalizable difficulty estimation tool, but may require significant training data and compute resources to achieve good performance.

TITLE: Model-Agnostic Prompt Difficulty Estimation using Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To improve the robustness of the model-agnostic predictor, we will explore using transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques to adapt the predictor to new models and tasks. This will involve pre-training the predictor on a large dataset of tasks and models, and then fine-tuning it on the specific task and model of interest. We will evaluate this approach on a range of tasks and models to demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness.
CONTROLS: Baseline: model-agnostic predictor without transfer learning or domain adaptation; Comparison: learned predictor trained on a specific model or task.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (~30 GPU-days of computation time for pre-training, fine-tuning, and evaluating the predictor).
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the robustness and generalizability of the model-agnostic predictor, but may require significant computational resources to pre-train and fine-tune the predictor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Rollout Generation using Prompt-Specific Budget Allocation with Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will develop a method that allocates rollout budgets to individual prompts based on an uncertainty estimate of the policy's confidence in its answers. This uncertainty estimate will be computed using a separate model that predicts the variance of the rollout returns. The method will adjust the rollout budget for each prompt to minimize the returned variance, ensuring that resources are allocated to the most informative prompts.
CONTROLS: Baseline: uniform rollout allocation; Ablation: no uncertainty estimation and uniform allocation.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (~15 GPU-days of computation time for training and evaluating the uncertainty predictor and rollout allocator).
PREDICTION: This approach should improve rollout efficiency and accuracy, but may over-allocate resources to uncertain prompts, leading to increased training time.

TITLE: Distributed Rollout Sampling and Data Parallelism for Large-Scale RL Training
PROPOSAL: To further scale up RL training, we will explore distributed rollout sampling and data parallelism techniques. By distributing the rollout sampling process across multiple GPUs or machines, we can significantly increase the throughput of rollout generation and reduce the memory requirements for training. We will evaluate this approach on a large-scale RL training task and compare its performance against a centralized rollout sampling approach.
CONTROLS: Baseline: centralized rollout sampling; Ablation: no data parallelism.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours (~45 GPU-days of computation time for training and evaluating the distributed rollout sampling and data parallelism techniques).
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve the scalability and throughput of RL training, but may introduce additional communication overhead and increase the complexity of the training process.

TITLE: Analyzing and Improving the Expressiveness of Model-Agnostic Prompt Difficulty Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the limitations of model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation and analyze the reasons behind its potential biases and inaccuracies. This will involve a detailed analysis of the training and testing datasets, as well as a comparison with human annotations and labels. Based on the insights gained from this analysis, we will propose and evaluate new techniques to improve the expressiveness and accuracy of model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation.
CONTROLS: Baseline: existing model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation techniques; Comparison: human annotations and labels.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (~10 GPU-days of computation time for data collection, analysis, and model retraining).
PREDICTION: This analysis should provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation, and lead to new techniques for improving its expressiveness and accuracy.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Model-Agnostic Prompt Difficulty Estimation on Multi-Task RL
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the applicability of transfer learning for model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation on multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) settings. We will develop a framework that allows the model to learn task-invariant features and adapt to novel tasks with minimal retraining. This will improve the robustness and generalizability of model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation across different RL tasks and environments.
CONTROLS: Baseline: task-specific difficulty estimation; Comparison: state-of-the-art transfer learning techniques.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (~25 GPU-days of computation time for training and evaluating the transfer learning framework).
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve the robustness and generalizability of model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation on multi-task RL settings, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and careful selection of meta-learning techniques.

PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation techniques on mathematical reasoning and retrieval-augmented multi-hop question answering tasks. We will compare our methods with state-of-the-art baseline techniques and analyze their performance on a range of evaluation metrics. This will provide a systematic assessment of the effectiveness of model-agnostic prompt difficulty estimation in improving the performance of RL models on complex reasoning and meta-learning tasks.
